questions.subject: Maths
questions.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 72°. What is the alternate angle on the other parallel line?
questions.why: Alternate angles form a Z-shape and are always equal, so the answer is 72°. The 108° option comes from confusing alternate angles with co-interior angles (which sum to 180°).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles, but its sides are not all equal length. What is the most specific name for this shape?
questions.why: A rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles but doesn't need equal sides — that's what makes it a rectangle rather than a square. Calling it a square is the common mistake of assuming right angles always mean equal sides.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: A student investigates whether the brand of battery affects how long a toy car runs for, keeping the toy car and the surface it runs on the same each time. Which variable is the controlled variable?
options: The surface the toy car runs on
How long the toy car runs for
The toy car itself, because it changes wear over time
questions.answer: The surface the toy car runs on
questions.why: The controlled variable is what you deliberately keep the same so it's a fair test — here, the surface (and the toy car) are kept constant. The brand of battery is the independent variable (what's changed), and run time is the dependent variable (what's measured); confusing 'kept the same' with 'what's measured' is the trap.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 130°. What is the co-interior (allied) angle on the other parallel line?
questions.why: Co-interior (allied) angles sit between the parallel lines on the same side and always add up to 180°, so 180° − 130° = 50°. Picking 130° is the classic slip of treating co-interior angles as equal, like alternate or corresponding angles.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.prompt: Which one of these statements about triangles is FALSE?
options: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60° angles.
An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides.
A right-angled triangle always has two equal sides.
A scalene triangle has no equal sides and no equal angles.
questions.answer: A right-angled triangle always has two equal sides.
questions.why: A right-angled triangle only needs one 90° angle — it can be scalene, isosceles, but never equilateral. The false statement wrongly assumes 'right-angled' automatically means 'isosceles', mixing up two separate ways of classifying triangles.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.prompt: Solve for x: 3(x + 4) = 21. A student says 'I'll subtract 4 from both sides first since it's inside the bracket.' Explain in one sentence why that's wrong, then give x.
questions.why: You must expand or divide first, because the 4 is multiplied by 3, not just added — dividing both sides by 3 first gives x + 4 = 7, so x = 3. Subtracting 4 straight away ignores the bracket's multiplier and breaks the balance rule.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: Your friend says: 'In an experiment testing whether the amount of exercise (minutes per day) affects heart rate, the type of exercise (running vs cycling) must be the dependent variable, because it's something that could also change.' Using an example of your own (not one already used this week), explain what actually makes a variable independent, dependent, or controlled, and correct your friend's mistake.
